props.title: Gold Diggers of Broadway
props.initialSlug: Showgirls chase love & fortune in glitzy musical

sections.content: **Gold Diggers of Broadway** (1929) stands as a pivotal early musical that showcased the rapid evolution of sound technology in Hollywood. Shot entirely in two-strip Technicolor, it represented Warner Bros' ambitious push into "all-talking, all-singing, all-dancing" entertainment following the success of **The Jazz Singer** (1927). The film's lavish musical numbers and backstage drama plot became a template that influenced decades of musicals, from **42nd Street** (1933) to **La La Land** (2016). While most of the film is now lost, with only fragments surviving, its impact on early sound musicals cannot be overstated.

sections.content: The film's director, Roy Del Ruth, expertly balanced the technical challenges of early sound recording with the demands of creating visual spectacle. The surviving footage reveals remarkable Technicolor sequences that pushed the boundaries of what was possible in 1929. The film's success spawned multiple remakes including **Gold Diggers of 1933** (1933), **Gold Diggers of 1935** (1935), and **Gold Diggers of 1937** (1937), each reflecting the changing aesthetics and social concerns of their respective years. SUBHEAD: Early Sound Musical Innovation

**Gold Diggers of Broadway** pioneered several technical innovations that became standard in movie musicals. The film used multiple cameras to capture dance numbers from different angles - a technique that wouldn't become common until **Flying Down to Rio** (1933) and other RKO musicals. The integration of musical numbers into the plot, rather than treating them as variety show segments, influenced later classics like **Singin' in the Rain** (1952) and **The Band Wagon** (1953).
